screens.title: Proactive Monitoring and Capacity Planning
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we shift from firefighting to planning. Proactive monitoring means continuously collecting meaningful signals so you can detect slow degradations, capacity limits, or unusual behavior before they become outages. Capacity planning uses that historic data to forecast needs and make deliberate decisions: scale up, scale out, or optimize what you already have. You will see concrete examples of monitoring agents, visualization stacks, and alerting rules that are both actionable and resistant to alert fatigue. We’ll also show how to preserve long-term data and use trend analysis and peak-load modeling to make confident infrastructure choices. A practical conceptual activity explains how a collector like collectd and a visualization tool like Grafana fit together and how to set a useful alert. By the end you’ll understand not only the what and the how, but the why: why retention matters for trend detection, why alerts must be precise, and why performance work is a continuous cycle. Think about a recent incident you handled — could historical metrics have given you an early warning? That question will guide the practice here.

screens.title: Why proactive monitoring matters
screens.narratorSegment: Proactive monitoring is the practice of continuously observing system signals so you notice slow change, not just obvious failures. A single pager that arrives when a database is down is reactive; proactive monitoring would have detected rising query latency and memory pressure hours or days earlier. Practically, this means choosing the right KPIs — C P U utilization, available memory, disk percent used, swap activity, interface errors, and load average — and tracking them over time. For example, if available memory trends downward month over month, you know to investigate application memory growth or to plan for more R A M before users see slowdowns. A common misconception is that adding more alerts equals better coverage. In fact, poorly chosen alerts create fatigue and mask real problems. A better approach is fewer, actionable alerts and a dashboard that reveals correlated spikes. This slide grounds the practice: monitoring without retention only helps the present; monitoring plus historical storage enables trend analysis and capacity planning. Your takeaway: treat monitoring as data collection for both immediate response and future planning. Ask yourself: what small trend today could become your outage next month?

keyIdea.text: Proactive monitoring captures current and historical signals so teams can detect slow degradations, not just failures, and plan capacity ahead of crises.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 10.10 › Why proactive monitoring matters
Definition & core idea

Proactive monitoring combines real-time alerting with long-term metric retention so teams can detect gradual regressions and forecast capacity needs.

Concrete example
Memory available decreases 5% monthly; planning adds RAM or optimizes application before outages occur.
Common misconception
More alerts are better — false. Excessive alerts cause fatigue and hide real incidents.
Why it matters
Prevention reduces downtime, improves UX, and enables planned resource investments.
Visual: KPI cards
CPU Utilization
Alert when sustained above 80% and trending upward over weeks.
Memory Available
Alert when available < 10% and watch swap activity for symptoms.
Disk %util
Critical disks above 90% need capacity action or cleanup.
Network errors
Rising rxerr/txerr rates signal hardware or cabling issues to investigate.
Key Takeaway

Measure now and store for later — only then can you detect trends and act before users notice problems.

screens.title: Agents and monitoring systems
screens.narratorSegment: Monitoring stacks split into collectors, storage/query layers, visualization, and alerting. Collectors like node_exporter, collectd, or Telegraf run on servers to gather metrics — C P U, memory, disk, network and process-specific counters. The storage layer holds those metrics: Prometheus scrapes endpoints and stores time-series, while other systems like InfluxDB provide different retention and write characteristics. Grafana is the visualization layer that can read Prometheus, InfluxDB, or other data sources to present dashboards that reveal trends and correlations. Enterprise systems such as Zabbix bundle collection, visualization, and alerting together, while Nagios or Icinga focus on availability checks with optional perf metrics. When choosing components, consider retention, query flexibility, and alerting capabilities. For example, Prometheus and PromQL are powerful for flexible queries and alerting rules, but require planning for long-term retention. A misconception is to treat agents as optional; without agents you have blind spots. Another trade-off is centralized vs. federated storage: centralization simplifies correlation but requires capacity for ingestion and retention. In practice, pick collectors that expose the metrics you need, a storage solution that supports your retention window, and Grafana for correlated visualization. Which combination best fits your environment depends on scale and retention needs.

Collectors (agents)
node_exporter
Prometheus exporter for OS metrics. Good for scrape-based architectures.
collectd
Plugin-based collector that can write to Graphite, Influx, or files for later ingestion.
Telegraf
Agent with many output plugins, often used with InfluxDB and Grafana.
Monitoring systems & trade-offs

Flexible querying and alerting; plan for long-term storage or remote write for retention.
Zabbix

Nagios / Icinga

Common trade-off

screens.title: Designing actionable alerts
screens.narratorSegment: Alerting is only useful when it leads to a concrete action. The design has three elements: the metric and threshold, the sustained duration, and the recipient or routing. For example, a C P U alert should not fire on a single spike. Alerting if C P U utilization stays above 80% for five minutes signals a sustained problem worth investigating. Memory alerts should be based on available memory or swap activity; available below 10% or continuous swap in/out are good vectors for alerts. Disk percent used needs a high threshold, such as 90% on critical volumes. Network errors should alert on rising rxerr or txerr counts rather than transient blips. Avoid alert fatigue by tuning duration windows and grouping related alerts so a single incident generates a coherent notification to a single on-call target. Routing matters: a C P U problem on a database host should go to the database team rather than the general ops channel. A common misconception is to prefer very low thresholds to be safe; this produces noise. Instead, prefer thresholds that are meaningful and paired with remediation steps. Lastly, alerts should be actionable: include clear context and a recommended first step. Ask yourself: when this alert fires, what is the first human step to resolve it?

keyIdea.text: Good alerts are precise, sustained, routed correctly, and paired with clear remediation steps to reduce noise and speed response.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 10.10 › Designing actionable alerts
Alert rule anatomy
Metric + Threshold
E.g., CPU > 80% averaged over 5 minutes.
Duration
Require sustained breaches to reduce false positives.
Routing
Send alerts to the team that can act, with a clear playbook link or step list.
Example alert templates
CPU sustained
Trigger when CPU > 80% for 5 minutes. Remediation: check processes, scale or optimize service.
Memory available
Trigger when available memory < 10%. Remediation: check swap activity and heavy processes.
Disk fill
Trigger when critical disk > 90%. Remediation: clean logs or increase capacity.
Pro Tip

Document expected remediation steps inside the alert so responders know the first actions to take and can reduce mean time to resolution.

screens.title: Collecting and visualizing historical data
screens.narratorSegment: Historical data is the foundation of capacity planning. Without retention you cannot detect monthly growth, seasonality, or slow regressions. Decide a retention window that matches your forecasting horizon: for many environments keep at least three months, but consider a year for seasonal businesses. Dashboards in Grafana let you visualize C P U, memory, disk input and output and network over time and overlay panels to check correlation. For example, a C P U spike combined with increased network traffic may indicate a batch job or a sudden workload shift. Good dashboards include context: host/service labels, time-range selectors, and panels that allow you to correlate metrics quickly. A misconception is to store everything at the highest resolution; instead, use downsampling or rollups for longer retention windows to balance storage and query performance. Also plan your queries for trend analysis: a simple monthly growth rate computation tells you if C P U usage grows by a percent per week or month. Finally, retention and dashboards enable peak-load analysis: identify daily or seasonal spikes to ensure capacity can absorb those peaks. Your takeaway: store what you need at an appropriate resolution and visualize correlated metrics to convert raw data into planning actions.

keyIdea.title: Retention & correlation
keyIdea.text: Store metrics for trend detection, downsample for long-term retention, and build dashboards that correlate metrics to reveal root causes and peak patterns.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 10.10 › Historical Data
Retention decisions
Choose retention based on how far ahead you plan: 3 months to 1 year are common. Use downsampling for older data to save space while preserving trends.
Three-month
Good for immediate trend detection and short-term capacity planning.
One-year
Helpful for seasonality and long-term projections.
Dashboard practices
Correlated panels
Overlay CPU and network to detect linked spikes and identify workload types.
Peak-load panels
Show daily/weekly peaks so you know required capacity during busiest times.
Contextual labels
Include host and service labels so panels can filter and compare similar targets.
Downsampling
Store high-resolution recent data and aggregated older data to balance cost and insight.
Key Takeaway

Retention plus correlated visualization turns raw metrics into actionable forecasts and root-cause signals.

screens.title: Capacity planning and trend analysis
screens.narratorSegment: Capacity planning converts observed trends into decisions about resources. Start with trend analysis: regularly review historical metrics to calculate growth rates — for example, C P U increasing by five percent per month. Use that rate to project when utilization will reach critical thresholds and plan actions before that point. Peak-load analysis identifies the busiest times, and you must ensure capacity for those peaks. Next, consider growth projections from the business: expected user growth or new features can change capacity choices. Model what-if scenarios: what if traffic doubles or memory per user increases by 20 percent? Use model outputs to choose between scaling up, scaling out, cloud bursting, or optimizing existing resources. Scaling up adds C P U or R A M to a server, while scaling out distributes load across more servers; cloud bursting temporarily adds cloud capacity during peaks. A common mistake is to treat capacity planning as one-time. Instead, treat it as ongoing: revisit projections at regular intervals and after major changes. The key is to prioritize options that match your operational model and budget. Ask: based on current trends and business forecasts, what is the most cost-effective path to avoid hitting critical resource limits?

keyIdea.title: Capacity core
keyIdea.text: Use trend analysis and peak-load modeling to project needs; choose scaling or optimization strategies based on those projections and business constraints.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 10.10 › Capacity Planning
Trend analysis steps
  1. Collect historical metrics over a consistent window.
  2. Compute growth rates (weekly/monthly) for each KPI.
  3. Project when KPIs will hit critical thresholds.
  4. Plan capacity actions using what-if scenarios.
Concrete example
If CPU grows 5% monthly and is at 70% now, plan a capacity action before it reaches 90%.
Scaling options
Scale Up
Add more CPU/RAM to existing servers for simplicity but limited elasticity.
Scale Out
Add more servers behind load balancers to distribute load.
Cloud Bursting
Temporarily add cloud resources to handle peaks without long-term cost.
Optimize
Improve efficiency by tuning application or identifying underutilized resources.
Key Takeaway

Project trends, run what-if scenarios, and pick scaling or optimization strategies aligned to business needs and cost models.

screens.title: The performance improvement cycle
screens.narratorSegment: Continuous performance improvement is a repeatable cycle. Start by monitoring: collect the right metrics continuously so you have data to analyze. Next, analyze the metrics to identify trends, anomalies, and correlations. Diagnosis follows: use profiling and deeper analysis to pinpoint the bottleneck, whether it's C P U saturation, inefficient queries, or input and output contention. Then tune: apply changes such as configuration adjustments, kernel or application optimizations, or hardware upgrades. After changes, test to verify the improvement in metrics and behavior. Finally, repeat: schedule regular reviews, update dashboards, and refine alerts based on lessons learned. For example, a quarterly review might reveal that C P U growth has accelerated with a new feature; that triggers profiling and either optimization or planned scaling. A common pitfall is skipping testing — assume changes help only after verifying with metrics and load tests. Another pitfall is one-off tuning without updating monitoring and alerts to reflect the new normal. Your role as an LFCE includes running these reviews and ensuring capacity plans keep pace with business changes. End with a simple commitment: set a cadence for reviews and tie them to upcoming projects so capacity planning remains proactive, not reactive.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 10.10 › Performance improvement cycle
Cycle steps
  1. Monitor: collect KPIs continuously and retain history.
  2. Analyze: spot trends, anomalies, and correlations.
  3. Diagnose: profile or inspect to find the bottleneck.
  4. Tune: apply configuration, software, or resource changes.
  5. Test: verify improvements under load or simulated traffic.
  6. Repeat: schedule reviews and update plans.
Scenario: new feature rollout
After a feature launch you see a 10% CPU increase. The cycle helps: monitor to confirm, analyze to find affected endpoints, diagnose with profilers, tune code or add capacity, test under simulated load, and then update the capacity plan.
Common mistake

Making one-off changes without updating monitoring or rerunning baselines risks regressions and hides the true impact of fixes.

screens.title: Conceptual activity: collectd and Grafana
screens.narratorSegment: This conceptual activity outlines practical steps to connect a collector to a visualization system. First, install collectd on a Linux server and enable plugins for C P U, memory, disk and network. In configuration files you enable plugins such as LoadPlugin C P U and LoadPlugin memory, then configure an output like WriteGraphite or WriteJSON so data can be sent to a time-series backend. Next, configure your storage or Prometheus ingestion so the metrics are retained for your desired window. In Grafana, add the data source and create panels for C P U, memory, disk input and output and network traffic. Ensure panels include labels for host and service so you can filter. Finally, add a basic alert — for example, C P U > 80% for 5 minutes — and route it to an appropriate notification channel. A common misconception is that the collector alone is enough; you need the dashboard and alerting rules to make collected data actionable. This conceptual exercise helps you map each component and understand the interactions before attempting full deployment in a lab or production environment. When you next see a metric, ask: where did it originate, where is it stored, and who should be notified if it breaks?

Module 11 › Chapter 10.10 › Collectd & Grafana (Conceptual)
Conceptual steps
  1. Install collectd and enable cpu, memory, disk, interface plugins.
  2. Configure output plugin (WriteGraphite or WriteJSON) to forward data.
  3. Set up time-series storage and define retention policy.
  4. Create Grafana dashboard panels and add alerting rules.
Sample collectd snippet
LoadPlugin cpu
LoadPlugin memory
LoadPlugin disk
LoadPlugin interface

screens.title: Assessment idea and practical decisions
screens.narratorSegment: Assessment helps you apply the concepts to real decisions. Consider a case where C P U utilization grows by roughly five percent per month for six months and now hits 70% during peak hours. This is a classic performance trend analysis example: sustained growth that threatens capacity. The immediate action is to initiate capacity planning. That involves projecting when C P U will hit critical levels, investigating root causes like inefficient code or increased workload, and deciding between optimization, scaling up, or scaling out. For an LFCE the right next steps are diagnostic profiling and planning: profile heavy processes to determine if optimization will suffice; if not, model scaling impacts. Also update alerts and dashboards so future growth is visible earlier. Another assessment question is picking KPIs and thresholds: prioritize C P U utilization, available memory, and network interface errors for real-time alerts. Reasonable thresholds might be C P U > 85–90% for sustained periods, memory available below 10–15%, and network errors rising above baseline. A common misstep is reacting to the current spike without modeling future growth. Instead, use the observed growth to choose a timed action that prevents reaching crisis levels. The learner question: given this trend, what combination of profiling, optimization, and scaling would you propose and why?

Assessment scenario
CPU grows 5% monthly for six months and now hits 70% at peak. This indicates a capacity trend needing planning: project when you will hit 90% and decide between optimization, scaling up, or scaling out.
Immediate actions
Profile processes and check for inefficient workloads.
Planning
Project time to critical threshold and schedule capacity actions ahead of that date.
Avoid this
Don’t apply short-term fixes without updating metrics and alerts.
Key Takeaway

Translate trends into concrete plans: profile, model, then choose scaling or optimization before users are impacted.

When an incident occurs, consult this checklist: do you have the historic data to analyze it, is the alert actionable, and what does the projection say about future capacity? If you can answer those questions, your approach is truly proactive and informed by data. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we shift from firefighting to planning. Proactive monitoring means continuously collecting meaningful signals so you can detect slow degradations, capacity limits, or unusual behavior before they become outages. Capacity planning uses that historic data to forecast needs and make deliberate decisions: scale up, scale out, or optimize what you already have. You will see concrete examples of monitoring agents, visualization stacks, and alerting rules that are both actionable and resistant to alert fatigue. We’ll also show how to preserve long-term data and use trend analysis and peak-load modeling to make confident infrastructure choices. A practical conceptual activity explains how a collector like collectd and a visualization tool like Grafana fit together and how to set a useful alert. By the end you’ll understand not only the what and the how, but the why: why retention matters for trend detection, why alerts must be precise, and why performance work is a continuous cycle. Think about a recent incident you handled — could historical metrics have given you an early warning? That question will guide the practice here.

These learning objectives define practical skills you will take away. First, you will understand why proactive monitoring prevents incidents and how long-term metrics support capacity planning. That context helps you stop reacting and start predicting. Second, you will be able to configure basic, actionable alerts for key performance indicators such as C P U, memory, disk utilization, and network errors, and you will know how to set thresholds that reduce noise while still catching real problems. Third, you will learn to collect and visualize historical performance data using collectors and dashboards so you can spot trends, correlate spikes across metrics, and build retention policies. Fourth, you will grasp the principles of capacity planning and continuous performance improvement: how to analyze trends, model what-if scenarios, and choose when to scale up, scale out, or optimize. Each objective includes a small mnemonic to anchor the skill and points you to the milestone that verifies competency. By the end you will be able to move from alerts to plans, and from data to decisions.

This second objectives slide focuses on practical verification and the reasoning behind each skill. You will learn to map KPIs to alert rules so that each alarm is tied to a remediation action. For example, an alert for available memory below 10% should lead to a checklist of immediate steps: review processes, check swap activity, and prioritize critical services. You will also practice building dashboards that correlate C P U, memory, disk input and output, and network to help you diagnose cause and effect. Another objective is retention planning: choose a retention window that balances storage cost with the need to detect long-term patterns, like steady C P U growth. Finally, you will adopt the continuous improvement cycle: schedule regular reviews where you analyze trends, test hypotheses, and validate tuning or scaling. This keeps capacity planning current as business needs and features change. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you can demonstrate the skill in a review or lab.

Proactive monitoring is the practice of continuously observing system signals so you notice slow change, not just obvious failures. A single pager that arrives when a database is down is reactive; proactive monitoring would have detected rising query latency and memory pressure hours or days earlier. Practically, this means choosing the right KPIs — C P U utilization, available memory, disk percent used, swap activity, interface errors, and load average — and tracking them over time. For example, if available memory trends downward month over month, you know to investigate application memory growth or to plan for more R A M before users see slowdowns. A common misconception is that adding more alerts equals better coverage. In fact, poorly chosen alerts create fatigue and mask real problems. A better approach is fewer, actionable alerts and a dashboard that reveals correlated spikes. This slide grounds the practice: monitoring without retention only helps the present; monitoring plus historical storage enables trend analysis and capacity planning. Your takeaway: treat monitoring as data collection for both immediate response and future planning. Ask yourself: what small trend today could become your outage next month?

Monitoring stacks split into collectors, storage/query layers, visualization, and alerting. Collectors like node_exporter, collectd, or Telegraf run on servers to gather metrics — C P U, memory, disk, network and process-specific counters. The storage layer holds those metrics: Prometheus scrapes endpoints and stores time-series, while other systems like InfluxDB provide different retention and write characteristics. Grafana is the visualization layer that can read Prometheus, InfluxDB, or other data sources to present dashboards that reveal trends and correlations. Enterprise systems such as Zabbix bundle collection, visualization, and alerting together, while Nagios or Icinga focus on availability checks with optional perf metrics. When choosing components, consider retention, query flexibility, and alerting capabilities. For example, Prometheus and PromQL are powerful for flexible queries and alerting rules, but require planning for long-term retention. A misconception is to treat agents as optional; without agents you have blind spots. Another trade-off is centralized vs. federated storage: centralization simplifies correlation but requires capacity for ingestion and retention. In practice, pick collectors that expose the metrics you need, a storage solution that supports your retention window, and Grafana for correlated visualization. Which combination best fits your environment depends on scale and retention needs.

Alerting is only useful when it leads to a concrete action. The design has three elements: the metric and threshold, the sustained duration, and the recipient or routing. For example, a C P U alert should not fire on a single spike. Alerting if C P U utilization stays above 80% for five minutes signals a sustained problem worth investigating. Memory alerts should be based on available memory or swap activity; available below 10% or continuous swap in/out are good vectors for alerts. Disk percent used needs a high threshold, such as 90% on critical volumes. Network errors should alert on rising rxerr or txerr counts rather than transient blips. Avoid alert fatigue by tuning duration windows and grouping related alerts so a single incident generates a coherent notification to a single on-call target. Routing matters: a C P U problem on a database host should go to the database team rather than the general ops channel. A common misconception is to prefer very low thresholds to be safe; this produces noise. Instead, prefer thresholds that are meaningful and paired with remediation steps. Lastly, alerts should be actionable: include clear context and a recommended first step. Ask yourself: when this alert fires, what is the first human step to resolve it?

Historical data is the foundation of capacity planning. Without retention you cannot detect monthly growth, seasonality, or slow regressions. Decide a retention window that matches your forecasting horizon: for many environments keep at least three months, but consider a year for seasonal businesses. Dashboards in Grafana let you visualize C P U, memory, disk input and output and network over time and overlay panels to check correlation. For example, a C P U spike combined with increased network traffic may indicate a batch job or a sudden workload shift. Good dashboards include context: host/service labels, time-range selectors, and panels that allow you to correlate metrics quickly. A misconception is to store everything at the highest resolution; instead, use downsampling or rollups for longer retention windows to balance storage and query performance. Also plan your queries for trend analysis: a simple monthly growth rate computation tells you if C P U usage grows by a percent per week or month. Finally, retention and dashboards enable peak-load analysis: identify daily or seasonal spikes to ensure capacity can absorb those peaks. Your takeaway: store what you need at an appropriate resolution and visualize correlated metrics to convert raw data into planning actions.

Capacity planning converts observed trends into decisions about resources. Start with trend analysis: regularly review historical metrics to calculate growth rates — for example, C P U increasing by five percent per month. Use that rate to project when utilization will reach critical thresholds and plan actions before that point. Peak-load analysis identifies the busiest times, and you must ensure capacity for those peaks. Next, consider growth projections from the business: expected user growth or new features can change capacity choices. Model what-if scenarios: what if traffic doubles or memory per user increases by 20 percent? Use model outputs to choose between scaling up, scaling out, cloud bursting, or optimizing existing resources. Scaling up adds C P U or R A M to a server, while scaling out distributes load across more servers; cloud bursting temporarily adds cloud capacity during peaks. A common mistake is to treat capacity planning as one-time. Instead, treat it as ongoing: revisit projections at regular intervals and after major changes. The key is to prioritize options that match your operational model and budget. Ask: based on current trends and business forecasts, what is the most cost-effective path to avoid hitting critical resource limits?

Continuous performance improvement is a repeatable cycle. Start by monitoring: collect the right metrics continuously so you have data to analyze. Next, analyze the metrics to identify trends, anomalies, and correlations. Diagnosis follows: use profiling and deeper analysis to pinpoint the bottleneck, whether it's C P U saturation, inefficient queries, or input and output contention. Then tune: apply changes such as configuration adjustments, kernel or application optimizations, or hardware upgrades. After changes, test to verify the improvement in metrics and behavior. Finally, repeat: schedule regular reviews, update dashboards, and refine alerts based on lessons learned. For example, a quarterly review might reveal that C P U growth has accelerated with a new feature; that triggers profiling and either optimization or planned scaling. A common pitfall is skipping testing — assume changes help only after verifying with metrics and load tests. Another pitfall is one-off tuning without updating monitoring and alerts to reflect the new normal. Your role as an LFCE includes running these reviews and ensuring capacity plans keep pace with business changes. End with a simple commitment: set a cadence for reviews and tie them to upcoming projects so capacity planning remains proactive, not reactive.

This conceptual activity outlines practical steps to connect a collector to a visualization system. First, install collectd on a Linux server and enable plugins for C P U, memory, disk and network. In configuration files you enable plugins such as LoadPlugin C P U and LoadPlugin memory, then configure an output like WriteGraphite or WriteJSON so data can be sent to a time-series backend. Next, configure your storage or Prometheus ingestion so the metrics are retained for your desired window. In Grafana, add the data source and create panels for C P U, memory, disk input and output and network traffic. Ensure panels include labels for host and service so you can filter. Finally, add a basic alert — for example, C P U > 80% for 5 minutes — and route it to an appropriate notification channel. A common misconception is that the collector alone is enough; you need the dashboard and alerting rules to make collected data actionable. This conceptual exercise helps you map each component and understand the interactions before attempting full deployment in a lab or production environment. When you next see a metric, ask: where did it originate, where is it stored, and who should be notified if it breaks?
